design_detail: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled physiological challenge study in a cardiac catheterization laboratory of an urban teaching hospital (University of Texas Southwestern / Parkland Memorial Hospital). 30 clinically stable patients undergoing catheterization to evaluate chest pain were randomized to intranasal saline (group 1, n = 15) or intranasal cocaine hydrochloride 2 mg/kg as a 10% solution (group 2, n = 15). Fifteen minutes later, 5 of the group 1 patients and all 15 group 2 patients received a 5-minute intracoronary infusion: propranolol 0.4 mg/min (total 2 mg) after saline (group 1A, n = 5) or after cocaine (group 2B, n = 10), or intracoronary saline after cocaine (group 2A, n = 5). The coronary sinus catheter paced the heart to hold heart rate constant so that neither investigator nor patient could tell which agent was infused. Outcomes at each step: heart rate, systolic and mean arterial pressure, rate-pressure product, coronary sinus blood flow by thermodilution, arterial-coronary sinus oxygen content difference, and quantitative arteriographic diameters of the proximal, mid and distal left anterior descending and left circumflex arteries. No patient had previously used cocaine; the comparison is therefore a drug challenge in cocaine-naive cardiac patients, not a trial of treatment in people presenting after cocaine use.
can_establish: That in 10 cocaine-naive patients under catheterization, 2 mg of intracoronary propranolol given 15 minutes after intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg was followed by a further fall in coronary sinus blood flow and a further rise in coronary vascular resistance, while a matched intracoronary saline infusion after cocaine (n = 5) and propranolol after intranasal saline (n = 5) were not; and that intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg raised arterial pressure and reduced coronary flow and epicardial diameters in 15 such patients.
cannot_establish: Whether systemically administered beta-blockers (intravenous or oral, the forms used in hospitals) harm people who present with cocaine-associated chest pain: the drug here went directly into the coronary artery at 2 mg in patients without coronary symptoms. Nor can it establish any clinical outcome (infarction, arrhythmia, death), the effect of cocaine doses or routes other than 2 mg/kg intranasally, the effect in people who use cocaine regularly (none had used it before), or that the potentiation is statistically reliable against the post-cocaine state, since the randomized between-arm comparison (group 2A versus 2B) was never tested and the within-person resistance change from the post-cocaine value had P = 0.074.

sample.recruitment: Clinically stable patients referred for cardiac catheterization to evaluate chest pain at an urban teaching hospital. 34 consecutive patients with stable symptoms and no exclusion criterion were eligible; 3 declined and 1 was excluded when initial angiography showed severe left main coronary artery disease, leaving 30 (p. 898).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: stable symptoms, undergoing catheterization for chest pain. Excluded: hypertension, recent myocardial infarction, history of pseudocholinesterase deficiency, and (after angiography) severe left main disease. Anti-anginal drugs, including beta-blocking agents, calcium antagonists and long-acting nitrates, were stopped more than 12 hours before the study; patients were studied fasting after 5 to 10 mg of oral diazepam (p. 898).
sample.demographics: 30 patients, 25 men and 5 women, aged 38 to 68 years. Group 1: 11 men and 4 women, 43 to 65 years. Group 2: 14 men and 1 woman, 38 to 68 years. Coronary anatomy of the whole sample: 7 angiographically normal, 11 one-vessel, 9 two-vessel and 3 three-vessel disease (70% or greater luminal narrowing of a large epicardial artery). No patient had a history of previous cocaine use (pp. 898-899).
sample.attrition: None reported after randomization; all 30 appear in the tables. Four of the 34 eligible patients did not enter the study (3 declined, 1 excluded on angiography) (p. 898).
sample.selection_effects: Older cardiac patients (mostly men) with chest pain under investigation, half of them with obstructive coronary disease and none with any cocaine experience, given a single controlled intranasal dose in a catheterization laboratory. This is the opposite of the population the finding is used about: people who use cocaine, often repeatedly and at much larger amounts, who arrive at an emergency department with chest pain. The authors themselves note that reported cocaine-associated infarctions follow amounts often above 1000 mg, far more than the 110 to 210 mg given here (p. 902). Patients were also pretreated with diazepam and had their own anti-anginal drugs withdrawn, and the 5:10 split of group 2 between intracoronary saline and propranolol is not explained.

exposure.measurement: Both drugs were given in the laboratory. Serum cocaine was measured by gas chromatography 15 minutes after dosing. Propranolol was infused into the left coronary artery, so no systemic concentration applies (p. 898).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only. Single intranasal dose of 10% cocaine hydrochloride solution, 2 mg/kg body weight (110 to 210 mg across patients), described by the authors as one half to two thirds the amount routinely used for topical rhinolaryngologic anesthesia and chosen for that reason; the resulting serum concentration was 0.097 +/- 0.051 mg/L (range 0.02 to 0.22 mg/L). Intracoronary propranolol 0.4 mg/min over 5 minutes (total 2 mg) or an equal-duration intracoronary saline infusion, begun 15 minutes after the intranasal dose (pp. 898-899).
exposure.polysubstance: All patients received 5 to 10 mg of oral diazepam as premedication before the study, and iodinated contrast for angiography; anti-anginal medication (beta-blockers, calcium antagonists, long-acting nitrates) was withdrawn more than 12 hours earlier. Other drug or alcohol use by the patients is not reported, and no toxicology screening is described (p. 898).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: no patient had used cocaine before the study (p. 898).

comparison.controls: Three comparisons are available. (1) Randomized, between-person: intranasal saline (n = 15) against intranasal cocaine (n = 15), for the effect of cocaine. (2) Randomized, between-person within group 2: intracoronary saline (n = 5) against intracoronary propranolol (n = 10) after cocaine. (3) Non-randomized, within-person: each group 2B patient's values after propranolol against the same patient's values after cocaine and at baseline, which is the comparison the paper's conclusion rests on.
comparison.matching: Randomization only; no matching, and no baseline comparison between groups 2A and 2B is reported or tested. Their printed baselines differ (coronary sinus blood flow 126 +/- 25 mL/min in group 2A against 139 +/- 28 in group 2B; Tables 3A and 3B, pp. 900-901). Heart rate was held constant by coronary sinus pacing during the infusions, which removes rate as a confounder of the flow change but also removes the main visible sign of beta-blockade.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable in the usual sense (no prior cocaine exposure). Unmeasured are each patient's coronary reactivity before the drug, their endothelial function, and whether the angiographic disease pattern was balanced between groups 2A and 2B; the sample's own disease counts are internally inconsistent (see reporting issues).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Control patients received the same premedication and contrast, and intranasal saline in place of cocaine; 5 of them also received intracoronary propranolol, which is the arm that shows propranolol alone did not reduce coronary flow (Table 2, p. 899).

outcomes.instruments: Coronary sinus blood flow by continuous thermodilution through a pacing thermodilution catheter placed via a basilic vein; systemic arterial pressure through the femoral arterial sheath side-port; heart rate by electrocardiographic monitoring; arterial and coronary sinus blood sampled for oxygen content; cineangiography of the left coronary artery in two orthogonal right anterior oblique projections, measured by computer-assisted quantitative coronary analysis (Cardiovascular Angiography Analysis System) at an image resolution of 3.8 line pairs/mm; coronary vascular resistance derived as mean arterial pressure divided by coronary sinus blood flow (pp. 898-899).
outcomes.validity_norms: Thermodilution gives total left coronary flow, not regional myocardial perfusion, as the authors state among their limitations (p. 901). Quantitative arteriography of six named segments is the standard method of the period; the authors report that all analyses were done without knowledge of which agent had been given (p. 898).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Potentiation' is operationalized as a further fall in coronary sinus blood flow and a further rise in coronary vascular resistance after intracoronary propranolol relative to the post-cocaine measurement, plus constriction greater than 10% in one or more epicardial segments. No ischemic clinical endpoint was prespecified; the one ischemic event is reported descriptively.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 13 counts the variables in each table (7 hemodynamic and metabolic measures and 6 arterial segments); each is tested at two or three time points in four groups, so well over a hundred paired tests are printed across Tables 1, 2, 3A and 3B, all at an uncorrected threshold of P < 0.05 (p. 899).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Stated: all hemodynamic and arteriographic analyses were done without knowledge of which agent (intranasal saline or cocaine, intracoronary saline or propranolol) had been given; patients and investigators were also blinded during administration, with pacing used to conceal the heart-rate effect of propranolol (pp. 898-899).

analysis.effect_sizes: Means +/- SE with 95% confidence intervals for mean change, paired t-tests, P < 0.05 as significant; no adjustment, no model, no effect sizes in standardized units (p. 899). Cocaine against saline (Table 1, p. 898): with intranasal cocaine, systolic pressure +11 mm Hg (5 to 16), mean pressure +9 (4 to 13), rate-pressure product +0.9 x 10^3 (0.4 to 1.4), coronary sinus blood flow -17 mL/min (-29 to -5), coronary vascular resistance +0.18 mm Hg/mL per min (0.13 to 0.24), transcardiac oxygen content difference +0.6 mL/dL (0.1 to 1.0); with saline, every change was within 1 unit of zero and no P value was below 0.27. Epicardial diameters after cocaine fell by 0.10 to 0.25 mm across the six segments, significant in four (P from 0.001 to 0.026) and not in the mid (P = 0.13) and distal (P = 0.087) circumflex. Editors' calculation from the Table 1 group 2 baselines and mean changes: the falls are 5.6% (proximal left anterior descending), 8.9% (mid), 10.2% (distal), 9.0% (proximal circumflex), 7.1% (mid) and 6.5% (distal). Propranolol after cocaine (group 2B, n = 10; Table 3B, p. 901, and text p. 899): coronary sinus blood flow 139 +/- 28 mL/min at baseline, 120 +/- 20 after cocaine and 100 +/- 14 after propranolol, a further fall of 15% +/- 18% (22% +/- 20% from baseline), mean change from the post-cocaine value -20 mL/min (-42 to -1), P = 0.050, and from baseline -40 (-77 to -2), P = 0.040; coronary vascular resistance 0.87 +/- 0.10, 1.05 +/- 0.10 and 1.20 +/- 0.12 mm Hg/mL per min, a further rise of 19% +/- 28% (46% +/- 44% from baseline), mean change from the post-cocaine value +0.16 (-0.02 to 0.33), P = 0.074, and from baseline +0.33 (0.12 to 0.53), P = 0.005. Saline after cocaine (group 2A, n = 5; Table 3A, p. 900): flow 0 mL/min (-8 to 8), P = 0.95, and resistance -0.08 (-0.18 to 0.03), P = 0.11, against the post-cocaine value. Propranolol after intranasal saline (group 1A, n = 5; Table 2, p. 899): flow -2 mL/min (-6 to 2), P = 0.19, and resistance +0.01 (-0.07 to 0.09), P = 0.66.
analysis.covariates: None. No adjustment for coronary disease severity, sex, age or baseline flow, and no test of whether groups 2A and 2B were comparable at baseline.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol, registration or prespecified primary outcome is mentioned; the study predates trial registration. Approved by the Human Subjects Review Committee of the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, with written informed consent after disclosure of possible adverse effects (p. 898).
analysis.selective_reporting: All four groups and all measured variables appear in the tables, which is unusually complete. The selectivity is in the summary rather than the data: the abstract gives the group 2B subgroup's values as the cocaine effect, states P < 0.05 for variables that Table 1 shows above 0.05, and states P < 0.05 for both propranolol effects when Table 3B gives P = 0.074 for the resistance change from the post-cocaine value (see reporting issues). The randomized comparison between groups 2A and 2B, the one comparison protected by randomization, is never tested.
analysis.power: The authors name low statistical power among their limitations, attributing it to the small number of patients (p. 902). The decisive comparison rests on 10 patients, with 5 as the saline control; the standard deviations around the percentage changes (18% and 28%) are larger than the changes themselves (15% and 19%).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In cocaine-naive patients undergoing catheterization, intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg raised blood pressure and rate-pressure product, reduced coronary sinus blood flow and narrowed epicardial segments, while intranasal saline changed nothing. In the 10 patients who then received 2 mg of propranolol into the coronary artery, flow fell further and resistance rose further relative to both the post-cocaine value and baseline, though the resistance change from the post-cocaine value had P = 0.074; in 5 patients given intracoronary saline instead, nothing changed further, and in 5 patients given propranolol after intranasal saline, nothing changed at all. Five of the 10 propranolol patients had an epicardial segment constrict by more than 10%, and one had a complete coronary occlusion with ischemic symptoms and ST elevation that resolved with sublingual nitroglycerin and left no rise in creatine kinase.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that cocaine-induced coronary vasoconstriction is potentiated by beta-adrenergic blockade and that beta-adrenergic blocking agents probably should be avoided in patients with cocaine-associated myocardial ischemia or infarction (p. 897); the closing paragraph repeats this for the patient with cocaine-induced chest pain and adds that nitrates or calcium antagonists may help, while noting they are not proved beneficial (p. 902). The distance between result and recommendation is large in three steps. First, route and setting: 2 mg of propranolol delivered directly into the left coronary artery of a cocaine-naive patient under catheterization is not the intravenous or oral beta-blocker a hospital gives, and the authors acknowledge they did not test other routes (p. 902). Second, outcome: the measured endpoints are flow, resistance and lumen diameter, not infarction, arrhythmia or death; the discussion's step from these to the magnitude of ischemia is reasoning, not measurement. Third, statistical support: the abstract's 'P < 0.05 for both' is not what Table 3B prints for the change from the post-cocaine state. The authors are otherwise careful, listing four limitations, reporting the one serious adverse event in full, and marking their statements about larger amounts of cocaine as unproven.

timeline.event: This study: intracoronary propranolol after intranasal cocaine further reduced coronary flow in 10 cocaine-naive catheterization patients

The same group gave intravenous labetalol (a combined alpha- and beta-blocker) after intranasal cocaine in 15 similar patients and found coronary vasoconstriction reversed rather than potentiated, while mean arterial pressure fell
American Heart Association scientific statement cites this study in recommending against beta-blockers in the acute setting of cocaine-associated chest pain
Registry comparison of hospitalized patients with cocaine-associated chest pain given or not given a beta-blocker: no difference in in-hospital outcomes
Meta-analysis of observational studies of beta-blocker use in cocaine-associated chest pain finds no increase in the pooled outcomes

replication.where_it_stands: The physiological finding has never been repeated in people who use cocaine, and no randomized trial of a systemic beta-blocker against placebo in cocaine-associated chest pain exists. What has accumulated since is observational hospital data, which do not show the harm this mechanism predicts, and the same group's own labetalol study, which found the opposite direction with a combined blocker. The mechanism stands; its clinical translation is contested.

funding.funder: Ischemic SCOR grant HL 17669 from the National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, Maryland, and a grant from the Texas Affiliate of the American Heart Association, Austin, Texas (p. 902).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the article (the journal did not require one in 1990).
funding.affiliations_note: All authors were in the Cardiology Division, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas. The same group produced the earlier study of cocaine-induced vasoconstriction and the later labetalol study, so the main line of human evidence on this question comes from one laboratory.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial in people presenting to hospital with cocaine-associated chest pain, comparing an intravenous beta-blocker with placebo or with an alternative such as a benzodiazepine or a nitrate, with infarction, arrhythmia, length of stay and death as outcomes and coronary flow or imaging in a subgroup. Short of that, a study giving an intravenous rather than intracoronary beta-blocker to people who actually use cocaine, at amounts they use, would close the route-and-population gap that separates this laboratory result from the bedside question.

domains.note: Patients were randomized twice (saline against cocaine, then intracoronary saline against propranolol within group 2) and the assignment was concealed from patient and investigator, with pacing used to hide propranolol's heart-rate effect. But the method of sequence generation and allocation concealment is not described, the unequal 5:10 split of group 2 is not explained, and no baseline comparison between groups 2A and 2B is reported, although their printed baseline flows differ by 13 mL/min.

Blinding appears to have held and no protocol deviations are reported. The concern is analytic rather than procedural: the conclusion is drawn from within-person before-after changes in group 2B rather than from the randomized contrast with group 2A, so the effect of time, of the preceding cocaine dose and of repeated instrumentation is not separated from the effect of propranolol by the randomization that was available.
All 30 randomized patients appear in the tables with no missing values reported; the one patient with coronary occlusion remained in the analysis.

Flow, pressure, oxygen content and lumen diameter are objective, and the analyses were done blind to the agent given. Thermodilution measures total rather than regional flow, which the authors state, but this does not bias the comparison between infusions.

No protocol or prespecified outcome; more than a hundred uncorrected paired tests across four groups. The abstract reports the 10-patient subgroup's values as the cocaine effect, attaches P < 0.05 to variables Table 1 shows at P = 0.13 and 0.087, and attaches P < 0.05 to both propranolol effects when Table 3B gives P = 0.074 for the resistance change from the post-cocaine value. The randomized between-arm comparison is never tested.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The physiology is carefully done and blinded, and the three-way control structure (saline then propranolol, cocaine then saline, cocaine then propranolol) is a genuine strength: it shows that neither propranolol alone nor the passage of time after cocaine reproduces the further fall in flow. The high rating comes from the selection of the reported result, which RoB 2 does not let the overall judgment fall below: the headline claim is stated with a certainty the tables do not carry, and the one randomized comparison that could have supported it was not analysed. The source can be cited for what intracoronary propranolol did to coronary flow, resistance and epicardial diameter in 10 cocaine-naive catheterization patients 15 minutes after intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg, for the absence of that change under intracoronary saline and under propranolol without cocaine, and for the single occlusion event. It cannot be cited for the effect of systemic beta-blockers on people who use cocaine, for any clinical outcome, or as evidence that beta-blockade is harmful at the bedside.

key_findings.finding: 30 patients undergoing catheterization for chest pain were randomized to intranasal saline (n = 15) or cocaine 2 mg/kg (n = 15); 25 were men, ages ran from 38 to 68 years, and no patient had a history of previous cocaine use.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods > Patients, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The intranasal dose was 110 to 210 mg of cocaine hydrochloride as a 10% solution, giving a serum concentration of 0.097 +/- 0.051 mg/L (range 0.02 to 0.22 mg/L) at 15 minutes; the authors chose it as one half to two thirds the amount used for topical rhinolaryngologic anesthesia.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods > Experimental Protocol, 2nd paragraph; Results > Propranolol-Treated Group (Group 2), 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: After intranasal cocaine (n = 15), systolic pressure rose 11 mm Hg (95% CI 5 to 16), mean pressure 9 (4 to 13), rate-pressure product 0.9 x 10^3 (0.4 to 1.4), coronary sinus blood flow fell 17 mL/min (-29 to -5) and coronary vascular resistance rose 0.18 mm Hg/mL per min (0.13 to 0.24); after intranasal saline (n = 15) no variable changed (all P >= 0.27).
Epicardial diameters fell after cocaine in all six measured segments, by 0.10 to 0.25 mm, significantly in four (P 0.001 to 0.026) but not in the mid (P = 0.13) or distal (P = 0.087) left circumflex.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the same rows: the falls correspond to 5.6%, 8.9% and 10.2% in the proximal, mid and distal left anterior descending and 9.0%, 7.1% and 6.5% in the circumflex, a wider range than the 6% to 9% the abstract gives.

key_findings.finding: No patient developed chest pain or electrocardiographic signs of ischemia after cocaine alone.

In the 10 patients given intracoronary propranolol 2 mg after cocaine, coronary sinus blood flow was 139 +/- 28 mL/min at baseline, 120 +/- 20 after cocaine and 100 +/- 14 after propranolol, a further fall of 15% +/- 18% (22% +/- 20% from baseline), and coronary vascular resistance was 0.87 +/- 0.10, 1.05 +/- 0.10 and 1.20 +/- 0.12 mm Hg/mL per min, a further rise of 19% +/- 28% (46% +/- 44% from baseline), with no change in rate-pressure product or transcardiac oxygen content difference.
key_findings.locator: Results > Propranolol-Treated Group (Group 2), 3rd paragraph (left column, continuing into the right column)
key_findings.note: Values are mean +/- SE. The percentage changes have standard errors larger than the changes themselves.

key_findings.finding: In Table 3B the propranolol change from the post-cocaine value was -20 mL/min (-42 to -1) for flow, P = 0.050, and +0.16 mm Hg/mL per min (-0.02 to 0.33) for resistance, P = 0.074; the changes from baseline were -40 mL/min (-77 to -2), P = 0.040, and +0.33 (0.12 to 0.53), P = 0.005.
key_findings.locator: Table 3B, coronary sinus blood flow and coronary vascular resistance rows (first row of each pair is the change from the post-cocaine value, second from baseline)
key_findings.note: This is the comparison the paper's conclusion rests on; for resistance it does not reach the paper's own threshold of P < 0.05.

key_findings.finding: In the 5 patients given intracoronary saline after cocaine, nothing changed further: flow 0 mL/min (-8 to 8), P = 0.95, and resistance -0.08 (-0.18 to 0.03), P = 0.11, against the post-cocaine value, while resistance remained raised against baseline (+0.13, 0.03 to 0.23, P = 0.021).
key_findings.locator: Table 3A, coronary sinus blood flow and coronary vascular resistance rows

key_findings.finding: In the 5 patients given intracoronary propranolol after intranasal saline, no hemodynamic or arteriographic variable changed: flow -2 mL/min (-6 to 2), P = 0.19, and resistance +0.01 (-0.07 to 0.09), P = 0.66.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, coronary sinus blood flow and coronary vascular resistance rows
key_findings.note: This arm is what separates an effect of propranolol on the cocaine-exposed coronary circulation from an effect of propranolol in general.

key_findings.finding: In 5 of the 10 patients given propranolol after cocaine (4 with and 1 without coronary artery disease), one or more epicardial segments constricted by more than 10%; in one patient a coronary artery occluded completely, with ischemic symptoms and ST-segment elevation, resolving after sublingual nitroglycerin with no rise in serum creatine kinase.
key_findings.note: Figure 1 (p. 902) shows the arteriograms of this patient; its legend states the lumen was reduced diffusely by 12% after cocaine, with the circumflex occluded after propranolol.

key_findings.finding: The authors list four limitations: thermodilution measures total rather than regional myocardial flow; only one cocaine dose and route was tested; only the intracoronary route of propranolol was tested; and the small number of patients gives low statistical power.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, limitations paragraph (begins p. 901, right column; continues p. 902, left column)

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that beta-adrenergic blockade potentiates the fall in coronary blood flow caused by cocaine and that beta-blockade probably should be avoided in the patient with cocaine-induced chest pain, adding that nitrates or calcium antagonists may help although this is not yet proved.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, summary paragraph (continuing into the right column)
key_findings.note: Recorded as the authors' recommendation about hospital care, not as a finding of the study; the study measured coronary flow, resistance and lumen diameter, not clinical outcomes.

reporting_issues.issue: The coronary anatomy counts for group 2 do not sum to its size: of the 30 patients, 3 of the 7 with normal arteries, 6 of the 11 with one-vessel disease, 5 of the 9 with two-vessel disease and all 3 with three-vessel disease are said to be in group 2, which totals 17 in a group of 15.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least two of the four subtotals are wrong, so the disease burden of the cocaine group, and its comparability with the saline group, cannot be established from the paper. This matters for reading the arteriographic results, since segment responses differed between patients with and without coronary disease.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the cocaine effect as coronary sinus blood flow falling from 139 +/- 28 to 120 +/- 20 mL/min and resistance rising from 0.87 +/- 0.10 to 1.05 +/- 0.10; these are the values of the 10-patient subgroup that later received propranolol, not of the 15 patients who received cocaine, whose values in the Results and Table 1 are 135 +/- 20 to 118 +/- 15 mL/min and 0.87 +/- 0.07 to 1.06 +/- 0.08.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader taking the abstract's numbers as the cocaine effect is quoting a subgroup of 10. The direction and approximate size are the same, so no conclusion changes, but the n behind the figures does.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states P < 0.05 for all the variables it lists as changed by cocaine, including coronary arterial diameters; Table 1 gives P = 0.13 for the mid and P = 0.087 for the distal circumflex. The abstract also gives the diameter fall as between 6% and 9%, while the Table 1 values correspond to 5.6% to 10.2% (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract presents the epicardial constriction as uniform and uniformly significant when two of six segments were neither. Claims about cocaine narrowing epicardial arteries should cite Table 1 segment by segment, not the abstract.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that propranolol further decreased coronary sinus blood flow and increased coronary vascular resistance with P < 0.05 for both; Table 3B gives P = 0.050 for the flow change and P = 0.074 for the resistance change measured from the post-cocaine value. Only the comparisons with baseline, which also contain the cocaine effect itself, reach P < 0.05.
reporting_issues.consequence: The study's central claim of potentiation is weaker in the table than in the abstract. Any claim that beta-blockade worsened cocaine-induced vasoconstriction should state which comparison it uses, and that the resistance change against the post-cocaine state did not reach the paper's own threshold in 10 patients.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 the distal left anterior descending row after intranasal saline reads -0.07 (0.41 to 0.28): the lower limit has lost its minus sign, so the printed interval runs backwards and does not contain its own point estimate.
reporting_issues.consequence: A typographical error in a control-arm row; the intended interval is almost certainly -0.41 to 0.28. It does not affect any conclusion but shows the tables were not fully proofed.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 3B the first propranolol row for the rate-pressure product reads -0.5 (-1.2 to 2.7). Every other interval in that table is centred on its point estimate; this one is centred on 0.75.
reporting_issues.consequence: One limit is likely mistyped. The variable is one the authors use to argue that myocardial oxygen demand did not change, so the imprecision falls on a supporting rather than a primary claim.

reporting_issues.issue: The group that received intracoronary propranolol after intranasal saline is called group 1A in the Methods and Results and group 1B in the Discussion.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader following the argument that propranolol alone does not reduce coronary flow has to infer that group 1B means the group 1A of Table 2; no group 1B is defined anywhere.

reporting_issues.issue: The randomized comparison between the patients given intracoronary saline after cocaine (n = 5) and those given propranolol after cocaine (n = 10) is never tested; every printed P value for the propranolol effect comes from within-person paired t-tests.
reporting_issues.consequence: The one contrast whose comparability randomization guaranteed is not reported, so the estimate of potentiation carries the risk of a before-after design (time after cocaine, repeated instrumentation) that the design had the means to avoid.
